summary: KAIRO helps farmers in India decide what to plant next. A farmer picks a state and district, or drops a pin on the map, then answers three simple questions: soil type, how the field is irrigated, and what was grown before. KAIRO reads NASA POWER daily weather records for that location, averages past kharif and rabi seasons, and compares them with crop needs from a sourced crop database. It recommends a two-season crop plan, explains why it may fit the field, names the main trade-off, and offers two alternatives. Every score can be inspected under "How this was calculated". KAIRO covers all of India through the nearest NASA weather grid cell and was tested in five Karnataka districts. It is decision support, not agronomic advice, and always tells users to check with a local agronomist. Saved plans can be reopened later.
details:
KAIRO is a crop-planning tool for farmers and local agronomists in India. A user chooses a state and district (or drops a pin on a map) and answers three questions: soil type, how the field is irrigated, and what was grown before. KAIRO then recommends a two-season plan (kharif, then rabi) with a best option, the reasons it may fit, the main trade-off, and two alternatives.

How it works: we downloaded NASA POWER daily weather (temperature, rainfall, humidity) for 882 grid points covering India, 2021–2026, and turned it into seasonal summaries. Each field uses its nearest NASA grid cell, and past kharif and rabi seasons are averaged. These are compared with crop needs in a sourced crop database using transparent rule-based scoring, then combined into rotations (a bonus for including a legume, a penalty for repeating a crop family). Every score can be opened under “How this was calculated”. A NASA GPM IMERG rainfall sample was used to cross-check rainfall.

Impact: KAIRO gives farmers local, plain-language guidance grounded in NASA data, and it shows its reasoning instead of acting as a black box. Saved plans let users return to earlier recommendations.

Tools: Python, Streamlit, pandas, Plotly, Folium with OpenStreetMap, SQLite, NASA POWER data, and Census 2011 district boundaries.

Creativity: a guided four-question flow, a trade-off-first recommendation, and an honesty-first design. Unverified crop data is flagged in the app, and KAIRO says it is decision support, not agronomic advice.

Limits: validated only in five Karnataka districts; six crops; some crop figures are still being verified; NASA POWER is modelled data for a ~56 km area, not a field measurement; no yield or savings claims are made.

AI use: built with Anthropic’s Claude (Claude Code), which assisted with code, tests and documentation. An optional feature can ask a hosted language model (Groq) to explain KAIRO’s results; its text is accepted only if every number matches KAIRO’s computed data.
